seo_title: KRANVOC | Entity Lore and Invocation Field Notes
description: A complete working guide to KRANVOC: what it is, the entity lore and invocation structure behind it, and the full protocol. Includes step-by-step protocol,...
keywords: how to work with a spirit
lede: Thirty days, three charges, and nothing. That is the shape of the failure this set of notes is about, and the reason it is worth writing down is that almost every experienced practitioner recognises it immediately while beginners find it genuinely puzzling and reach for the wrong conclusion. A silent month has at least three possible causes, they look identical from the inside, and each one calls for a different next move. The first is an office that was far too wide to be checkable. The second is a charge that was never actually charged. The third is a name with no document behind it at all. This piece goes through how to tell them apart, why the diagnosis matters more than the entity, and how a second charge with a narrower office differs from simply trying harder.

p: The office written at the start was four clauses long and could have been satisfied by almost any month in which nothing catastrophic occurred. That is the single most consequential detail in this account and it was not noticed until the day-thirty review, when the reviewer could not tell whether the criterion had been met. An office you cannot fail is not an office. It is a description of a mood.

The charge itself was given twice, both times sitting down, both times without interruption, and both times the practitioner noticed partway through that they were producing a feeling rather than holding a connection. The first was treated as a settling-in period. The second was treated as the actual charge. Both of those readings were reasonable and both turned out to be generous, which is the sort of error that only becomes visible later.

sections.h2: Three explanations for a silent month
p: One: the office was too wide, so there was nothing specific for the charge to attach to. Two: the charge was weak, so even a specific office had nothing holding it. Three: the name carries no information, so there was never a pattern present to interrupt in the first place. All three produce identical external experience, which is why the temptation is to conclude that the practice does not work and the temptation is wrong.

There is a fourth possibility that practitioners rarely name. The working was fine and the result is simply outside the window you chose. That one cannot be excluded in advance, and it is the reason the review cycle has a length rather than an endpoint. But it is the explanation you are entitled to consider last, after the three diagnosable ones have been ruled out, because it is the one that lets you stop looking.

sections.h2: How to tell a wide office from a weak charge
p: Start with the office, because it is on paper and can be examined without any metaphysics. Write it out again and ask the competent-person question: could someone who knew nothing about this work say what outcome would count as a miss? If the answer is no, the office is the problem, and no amount of additional charging will fix a criterion that cannot be failed.

Then examine the charge, which requires a harder and less popular test. Watch yourself the next time you sit down with the glyph, and note whether your attention actually left. It will leave, several times, and the question is what you do next. If you notice and return, the charge is sound and simply needs repetition. If you notice and then sit out the remaining minutes, the charge was not held, and no office in the catalogue will make that produce a result.

sections.h2: What a second charge with a narrower office looks like
p: The correction is usually unglamorous. Three clauses become one. Four nouns become one. The version you would have been embarrassed to write, because it seemed too small to be worth a working, is usually the correct one. A second charge performed on a properly narrowed office takes twenty minutes instead of an hour and produces a considerably clearer result than the first three charges combined, which is uncomfortable and also completely predictable.

The reason is mechanical. The charge works by holding one thing in mind, and a wide office does not fit in that space, so the attention distributes and the connection thins out. Narrowing the office is not a reinterpretation of the first working. It is a different working, and the honest thing to do with the first one is to record it as superseded rather than quietly counting its results.

sections.h2: The bookkeeping that survives a bad month
p: Four lines, written the same day, and kept without revision: the office as it was written, the date and length of the charge, the number of maintenance days actually completed, and one sentence describing the state of attention at the start of the charge. That is the whole record. It is short enough to be completed on a bad evening, which is the actual test of whether a bookkeeping system is any good.

Two things to keep out. Do not record interpretations, because a month with no events will generate a great many and all of them will be retrospective. And do not record anything that could be called evidence of contact, because at thirty days a practitioner is at their most willing to find something and least able to judge whether they found it. The four lines are enough to diagnose and not enough to delude.

The things that get reported in month one are almost always ordinary: a coincidence in timing, a dream with a relevant image, a change in mood, a stranger saying something that could be read as relevant, an existing intention suddenly feeling more urgent. None of these are diagnostic, and each of them is more likely to be produced by the attention now pointed at them than by anything else.

There is a useful asymmetry here. A genuine effect that is not going to show up in month one is not going to be distinguishable from coincidence in month one either, so there is nothing to be gained by looking. A pattern that is only visible to the person looking is, by construction, not a pattern. The honest position at thirty days is that the month has told you about your bookkeeping and not about your working, and those are different lessons.

sections.h2: What to do with the first version, formally
p: Write it off in the notebook, in one line, with the date. Not a ritual closure, not a burning, just a line saying the office was too wide and this attempt is superseded. Ritualising the failure is the fastest route to a practice made entirely of failed workings, and it also removes the useful information, which is that the first office was bad and the second one might not be.

Then write the replacement office, and require it to be shorter than the original. A shorter second office is the single most reliable improvement available at this stage, and it costs one evening. Most practitioners who take that evening get more from the following month than they did from the previous three charges combined.

sections.h2: The two conversations worth having with yourself
p: The first is about what you actually wanted. Sit with the question of whether the working was aimed at something you would welcome arriving, because a working pointed at a change you do not want has a different failure mode and a different ethical shape, and a surprising number of silent months turn out to have that at the bottom. This is worth doing before the second charge rather than after.

The second is about what the month was for. If the honest answer is that the month gave you a better record-keeping habit and a sharper sense of which aims are checkable, then something was delivered and it was not nothing. If the honest answer is that the month gave you nothing except an argument to have with your own practice, then the next step is a smaller working, not a stronger one.

sections.h2: How this differs from a working that simply failed
p: A failed working had a well-formed aim, a proper charge, completed maintenance, and a clear result that did not arrive. This account has none of those in order. That distinction is not a comfort; it means the thirty days carried less information than a genuine failure would have, and the correct response to that is a better-specified attempt rather than a conclusion about the practice.

Practitioners who keep these two categories apart tend to keep practising, and practitioners who collapse them tend to abandon or escalate. The escalation pattern is worth naming: after a silent month the most common next move is a more elaborate working with more entities and a more dramatic office, which produces a second silent month with an even worse record behind it.

sections.h2: Keeping the record, or burning it
p: Keep it. A working that produced no result is still the best available evidence about your own working conditions, because it is the only one where you have a complete and unvarnished account of what you did. Over a few of these, a clear pattern emerges about which of your four lines is usually the weak one, and that pattern will not emerge from the workings that succeeded.

The only case for discarding a record is if keeping it will feed the compulsive-appeal pattern, where the working is restarted on the strength of an ambiguous month. If that is a live risk for you, keep the four lines and discard the narrative, since the four lines carry the diagnosis and the narrative is what tempts the restart.

sections.h2: What the practice is after month three
p: By the third cycle, the useful output is not a result. It is a specification of how you actually operate: how long your charges really need to be, how many maintenance days you actually complete, which of your aims turn out to be unfalsifiable, and how quickly your office words inflate under the pressure of wanting something to be true. That specification is worth more than a single success, because it applies to every working you will ever run.

The temptation at month three is to raise the stakes, either by aiming higher or by becoming more elaborate. The more productive move is the opposite: make the next aim smaller and the record more honest. The people who get real results out of this material over years are not the ones who escalated, they are the ones who kept the aims small enough to be wrong.

faq: How do I tell whether the office was too wide or the charge was weak?

Test the office on paper first, by asking whether a stranger could say what outcome would count as a miss. If they cannot, the office is the problem. If they can, then watch yourself during the next charge and note whether your attention actually returns when you notice it has left, because a charge you keep restarting is a charge that was never held.
Is a month with nothing a sign the practice does not work?

Not on its own, and the month is even less informative than it looks, because a month with no events cannot distinguish a weak practice from a genuinely non-random situation. The useful move is to diagnose the office and the charge, narrow the aim, and run a second cycle. Concluding from a single silent month is the most common reasoning error in this area.

Four lines, written the same day: the office as written, the date and length of the charge, the number of maintenance days actually completed, and one sentence on your state of attention at the start. Leave out interpretations and anything that could be called evidence of contact, since a quiet month generates plenty of both retrospectively.
Should I escalate after a silent month?

No, and this is the characteristic mistake. The usual response is a more elaborate working with more entities and a more dramatic office, which makes the second record worse rather than better. Narrowing the aim is the change that produces information, and a smaller office is also the one that can actually be failed.
Is it worth keeping the record of a working that produced nothing?

Yes, and it may be the most useful record you keep, because it is the only one with a complete account of what you actually did. Across several of these the weak line becomes obvious. The exception is if keeping it will feed a compulsion to restart on the strength of an ambiguous month, in which case keep the four factual lines and discard the narrative.
